name: Artichoke Nibbles
headnote: Sunset presents this as a reader-contributed recipe from 1971 that became a standing favourite, the kind passed down in family memory books. It is essentially a savoury custard: eggs bind chopped marinated artichokes, sharp cheddar and bread crumbs, and the reserved artichoke marinade is used to saute the onion and garlic so none of that seasoned oil is wasted. Baking it set but not dry gives squares (or muffin-tin rounds) that hold together at room temperature, which is why it works as a make-ahead appetiser.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS — no reader comments or ratings shown on the page.
flags: Ingredient-for-ingredient match with the family version: 2 jars (6 oz) marinated artichoke hearts, 1 onion, 1 garlic clove, 4 eggs, fine dry bread crumbs, oregano, hot pepper sauce, sharp cheddar, 2 T minced parsley. Sunset 1971 is the documented origin of this dish and the family copy is a direct descendant. Collection recorded no source, so nothing to contradict.

name: Brownies
headnote: Patty Anderson writes this up as the plain, reliable brownie from the Fannie Farmer Cookbook, offered without embellishment because it does not need any. The whole thing is mixed in the pan the chocolate and butter were melted in, so there is one dish to wash and no creaming step, which is what makes it a standing family recipe rather than an occasion bake. Nuts are treated as optional.
comment_digest: One reader found the vanilla quantity too high and cut it to two teaspoons with good results. Another had lost their own old Fannie Farmer copy in the Hurricane Harvey flooding and was using this page to recover the recipe — an indication of how closely it tracks the printed original.
flags: Right cookbook (explicitly the Fannie Farmer Cookbook, which is exactly what the collection records) and clearly the same recipe: the blog's version is a scaled-up pan, with chocolate, butter, flour, walnuts and salt all exactly double the family's 3 oz / 6 T / 3/4 c / 3/4 c / 1/4 t. Not provably the identical printing: sugar is 2 3/4 c where double would be 3 c, and eggs are 4 where the family has 3 (double would be 6). Also a personal blog rather than an authoritative Fannie Farmer page, and no official one exists. Note the Seattle Times 'Fannie Merritt Farmer style' result is the 1896 Boston Cooking-School original, a different and much cakier recipe — not this one.

name: Brussels Sprouts -- Braised
headnote: The test kitchen landed on braising as the best treatment for sprouts because it draws off bitterness while keeping the colour bright and the texture tender rather than squeaky. Nothing is needed but water and salt in a covered pan, which is the point — the method beat microwaving and other shortcuts in their testing without adding a single extra ingredient. Seasoning is left until after draining so the sprouts are not watered down.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS — rating shown but no reader comments on the page.
flags: Exact match. ATK's ingredient list is 1 lb Brussels sprouts (stem ends and discoloured leaves removed) and 1/2 tsp table salt, with the 1/2 cup water in the method — identical to the family's 1 lb / 1/2 t salt / 1/2 c water, and the family's directions (boil covered, shake the pan, 8-10 min, drain, season with butter/salt/pepper) track the ATK method step for step. Collection records '2004 The New Best Recipe Book, ATK' and this is that recipe in ATK's own archive. Page is subscription-gated for full text but the headnote, ingredients and rating came through.
